Which Experiences Are Linked to Lower Hospital Ratings?
section: Financial and access processes deserve direct attention
text:
Financial and access processes deserve direct attention
Negative billing mentions have an adjusted association of −1.05 stars, followed by front-desk conduct (−0.97), scheduling (−0.92) and waiting (−0.90). These are the four largest negative-mention estimates in the primary model.
The model compares feedback within the same Google listing and accounts for the other positive and negative topic mentions, text length, year and contributor group. It uses 195,616 reviews after removing listings represented only once. An adjusted association describes a difference in ratings conditional on those recorded features; it does not compare identical care experiences.
The useful finding is that financial and access concerns retain information about dissatisfaction even when the recorded clinical and interpersonal topics enter the comparison. A hospital team therefore has a reason to examine these parts of the experience directly. They can remain important questions even when clinical interactions receive praise elsewhere in the feedback.
The categories point to different situations. Billing covers charges, disputes, payment and collections. Front-desk conduct concerns administrative interactions. Scheduling describes appointment access, while waiting concerns the timeliness of the care process. Grouping all four under a broad experience score would make it harder to determine which process and supporting records need examination.
For a service lead, the next step is to identify which of those situations appears in validated local accounts. An unexpected charge, a difficulty obtaining an appointment and a dismissive administrative interaction require different investigation questions. The association identifies a topic worth examining; the account establishes what the person actually describes and what evidence could clarify it.

Explore the adjusted associations, including their uncertainty Dots are model estimates; lines are 95% confidence intervals clustered by listing. Start with the six largest associations in either direction, or show every topic. Hover for full topic names and mention counts.

Treat these results as a prominent group of signals. Weighting the sample toward the eligible source corpus retains the same top-four group but swaps the order of waiting and scheduling. Closely spaced estimates should not become a rigid league table. The intervals describe model uncertainty and do not include label errors or selection into writing feedback.

The distinction matters when deciding where to spend investigative effort. A strong rating association identifies a concern that distinguishes dissatisfaction after recorded context is considered. A frequent topic provides a larger recurring set of experiences to understand. Local frequency, the situation described and the relevant process evidence are needed to turn either signal into a practical priority.
The raw rating gaps alone offer little separation: 23 of the 29 topics fall between −1.9 and −2.3 stars. A single low-rated account can contribute to several of those gaps. The chart shows what changes when the model considers the topics together.

Billing and cleanliness have raw gaps of −2.25 and −2.04 stars; their adjusted associations are −1.05 and −0.43. Similar raw gaps can therefore accompany different relationships after other recorded features enter the comparison. The connecting lines show two statistical comparisons, rather than a division of responsibility for the low rating.
A useful local question is whether a recurring concern points to a defined process problem that can be investigated. For waiting, that could mean identifying the stage people describe and comparing it with available waiting-stage records. For billing, it could mean distinguishing charge accuracy, disputed coverage and an unclear explanation. Those are proposed applications to test against local evidence. Multiplying review counts by coefficients would not estimate the number of affected patients, recoverable stars or the return from a change.

title: Which Experiences Are Linked to Lower Hospital Ratings?
section: A smaller coefficient can sit inside a very negative account
text:
A smaller coefficient can sit inside a very negative account
Negative safety mentions have an adjusted association of −0.64 stars. Yet 6,787 of the 7,377 accounts containing a negative safety mention, or 92%, have a one- or two-star rating. And 6,282, or 85%, contain at least one other topic mentioned negatively. Safety concerns are often embedded in accounts describing several sources of dissatisfaction.
Equitable-treatment concerns show a related pattern: 94% of the 4,266 accounts mentioning the topic negatively have a one- or two-star rating, while its adjusted association is −0.74 stars. These labels identify reported concerns and perceptions; they do not establish verified safety events or discrimination.
This context explains why a coefficient cannot stand in for the significance of an account. The overall rating summarizes the experience, while the model estimates the recorded topics jointly. Several concerns can share the same low rating, and a reviewer cannot choose a value below one star. A smaller adjusted coefficient can coexist with a strongly negative description.
The data do not isolate how much of a particular coefficient’s size is due to the rating floor, shared topics or other differences between accounts. The practical lesson is to preserve the concern and its surrounding context when feedback is summarized. Ranking only by adjusted stars could leave a safety, fairness or privacy issue less visible even though its substance merits specific assessment.
For those accounts, the next decision comes from human reading, label validation and appropriate supporting evidence. The question is what was reported, what needs verification and which existing service or quality process should assess it. The rating association remains useful context, while the significance of the particular concern requires its own judgment.

title: Which Experiences Are Linked to Lower Hospital Ratings?
section: Positive feedback shows what is worth understanding and preserving
text:
Positive feedback shows what is worth understanding and preserving
Bedside manner is mentioned positively in 66,094 accounts, or 33.7% of the labeled frame, with an adjusted association of +1.02 stars. Switch the coefficient chart above to “Positive mentions” to explore this complementary picture.
The large body of favorable descriptions gives hospital teams material for learning what people value in clinical interactions. The category includes empathy, respect, listening and interpersonal conduct. The model does not distinguish which specific behavior accounts for the association, so a useful next step is to read validated positive examples in a comparable service and identify the conduct they describe.
The largest positive point estimate belongs to behavioral health (+1.07 stars), but it comes from 979 positive-mention accounts, compared with 66,094 for bedside manner. Their confidence intervals overlap. Both may supply valuable examples, with different scopes; the slightly larger coefficient does not establish a universally stronger learning opportunity.
Positive and negative signals also need separate interpretation. Billing’s negative association is −1.05 stars and its positive association +0.50; scheduling’s are −0.92 and +0.46. The model estimates praise and complaints as separate features. Removing a complaint does not automatically produce the experience described in a positive account, and silence about a topic does not establish satisfaction with it.
For improvement work, this creates a second question alongside investigating dissatisfaction: what do people value that a proposed change should preserve? A team could select a small set of validated positive accounts from the relevant service, identify recurring behaviors and choose a specific practice to examine or test. The association helps select material for that learning; it does not supply a tested protocol or predict the rating gain from adopting it.

section: Use the signals to choose the next question
text:
Use the signals to choose the next question
The findings support three questions for a hospital deciding where to look more closely:

Which experiences distinguish dissatisfaction? Use the adjusted associations to identify topics that remain informative after the recorded context is considered.
Which concerns recur in our own service? Use local feedback counts, periods and service context to locate a recurring set of experiences.
Which accounts need specific assessment because of what they describe? Preserve the full concern and use relevant verification, irrespective of its position in a rating ranking.

For example, a hospital noticing recurring billing concerns could first establish what is disputed: the amount, the coverage decision or the explanation. That determines which records and participants are relevant. Only after clarifying the problem can a team choose a response and a measure of whether it helped. The national association supplies a reason to look; it does not select the local solution.
If a process changes, evaluate it using appropriate independent process and experience evidence, alongside what subsequent feedback describes. A change in review volume or star ratings alone can also reflect who contributes and which services are represented. Positive accounts can help specify what the revised process should preserve.
The topic-pair article adds another useful question: which linked concerns need to be read together? Their shared context matters for follow-up. The number of complaints in an account is not a linear measure of rating damage; the supporting interaction check below explains why.


Do connected complaints bring an additional rating penalty?

Five selected pairs, including billing with insurance and waiting with staffing, were examined in two listing halves. Each model includes the usual topic indicators and controls, plus total topic count and a term for each pair of negative mentions. That interaction is the additional association beyond the two separate terms.

Lines show 95% confidence intervals clustered by listing. Values above zero indicate less negative associations than an additive model would predict.

All five holdout estimates are positive, ranging from +0.19 to +0.74 stars, with individual 95% intervals above zero. The combined association is less negative than simple addition predicts. This describes a bounded rating model; it does not mean two concerns improve the experience or are less serious. It cannot establish the benefit of preventing a second problem.
Pair selection used the earlier co-occurrence analysis of the broader dataset, so the split is not fully independent validation of discovery. Both halves are fitted separately. The displayed intervals are individual intervals, without a simultaneous correction across the five pairs.



How stable are the rating signals?

The checks support the broad pattern across alternative weighting and rating specifications. Weighting retains billing, front-desk conduct, scheduling and waiting as the top-four negative-mention set, while waiting and scheduling exchange order. These results favor interpreting a group of prominent signals over assigning importance to small ranking differences.

The following original plot compares all 29 negative-topic estimates. The vertical axis is an association in percentage points from a low-versus-high rating model, rather than an overall probability of a low rating. Like the linear stars model, a linear probability model can produce predictions outside the outcome’s bounds.

Source: saved low-versus-high robustness model. It drops three-star reviews and uses the same topic indicators, listing effects and controls as the primary model. Weighting does not remove self-selection into reviewing, and the simpler ordinal check does not validate all features of the primary specification. None replaces human validation of the labels.



Methods, contributor comparison and aggregate data

Sample and units. The 217,343-review coverage sample spans 2019 to early June 2026. Of these, 196,183 reviews at 9,904 Google listings have at least one validity-gated label. The primary model retains 195,616 reviews at 9,337 listings after singleton removal. A review is keyed by listing plus review ID. Counts and shares in the text and coefficient tooltips refer to the full labeled frame; interaction counts refer to the corresponding split before singleton removal. Listings are not necessarily distinct physical hospitals.
Model and comparison. Ordinary least squares models the 1–5-star rating using 58 binary topic–sentiment indicators, log(1 + review word count), year and contributor-group indicators, and listing fixed effects. A topic can have both a positive and a negative flag; neutral statements set neither. For a raw negative-mention gap, the reference group has neither directional flag for that topic and can include neutral-only mentions. The raw and adjusted comparisons have different conditioning and slightly different populations, so their difference is not a causal decomposition. Listing effects account for stable differences between listings, rather than changing service or reviewer mix within them. Intervals are 95% and clustered by listing. R² is 0.782, an in-sample fit measure rather than predictive performance on new feedback.
New context checks. Negative-mention reach divides distinct negative-topic accounts by all 196,183 labeled reviews. Low-rating concentration divides one- and two-star negative-topic accounts by all accounts mentioning that topic negatively. Additional-negative-topic share records whether another topic also has a negative flag in the same account. These are descriptive context measures, not patient prevalence or estimates of verified incidents.
Contributor comparison. In this labeled frame, the correct multi-listing-minus-single-listing contrast is −0.0068 stars with listing effects alone (95% interval −0.0315 to +0.0178), and +0.0277 in the full primary model (+0.0147 to +0.0408). The adjusted difference is small and positive, with its interval excluding zero under the model. The contrast subtracts the two group coefficients using their full clustered covariance; their common omitted reference is the 11+ group. It does not establish identical experiences or explain away the different population comparison in Whose Voices Shape Hospital Ratings.
Interpretation. Topic labels describe the text accompanying the observed rating. Their associations are therefore diagnostic of the same reported experience. Automated validity checks establish source and format matching, not human agreement. Public feedback is self-selected; model intervals do not cover label errors, missing experiences or selection bias. The labels do not verify clinical events. Coefficients cannot serve as severity weights or expected intervention returns.
Data and reproducibility. Download the original aggregate chart estimates or the additional counts, context measures and verified contrasts. The original charts retain the executed notebook’s saved values, rounded to four decimals. scripts/generate_hospital_rating_insights.py reconstructs the frozen review-level inputs, recomputes the new descriptive measures and refits the primary, weighted, low/high and pair models for reconciliation. Their estimates match the saved chart precision. The ordinal model was inspected in the executed notebook and not refitted in this check. Exports contain no raw review text, contributor identifiers or listing identifiers.

section: Understand the setting behind the rating gap
text:
Understand the setting behind the rating gap
Repeat contributors give 3.50 stars on average, compared with 3.74 among single-listing contributors. About 73% of that gap sits in listing mix: approximately 0.173 of the 0.237-star difference. The within-listing component is 0.061 stars, with a small remainder.
Single-listing contributors also rate the repeat group’s mix of places lower than their own overall average. The pooled difference therefore contains information about where feedback comes from, as well as how people assess their experience.

Most of the group rating gap reflects which listings receive feedback Repeat profiles (2–10 listings) minus single-listing profiles. The listing-mix, within-listing, and remaining components add to the overall gap; negative values indicate a lower repeat-profile mean.

Similar ratings can describe different experiences
The separate topic sample contains 176,853 labeled reviews at 7,776 listings represented by both groups: 152,703 single-listing and 24,150 repeat contributions. The direction persists in both bands. For equitable treatment, the 4–5-star shares are 0.36% versus 0.62%. The ratio is sizeable, but the absolute difference is about a quarter of a percentage point. What that difference means for a hospital depends on the situations those accounts describe.

title: Whose Voices Shape Hospital Ratings
section: Turn the topic signal into a question about the experience
text:
Turn the topic signal into a question about the experience
The aggregate data locate subjects for closer reading. To learn what a hospital could change, a team needs to distinguish the concrete situations grouped under each label. The full topic definitions provide a starting point:









Signal
What to clarify in the accounts
Follow-up




Accessibility and accommodations
Physical access, mobility support, interpretation, or sensory communication accommodations?
Validate the described barrier and involve the relevant facilities, access or communication team.


Equitable treatment
What interaction was perceived as biased or unfair, and in which service context?
Examine the account and relevant contextual evidence through existing review processes.


Patient safety and errors
What error, omission or harm concern was reported?
Assess serious concerns through the existing quality/safety route, independently of the star rating.


Care coordination and referrals
Where did a referral, transfer, handoff or follow-up lose information or responsibility?
Review the described sequence with the relevant service teams.




These are investigation questions informed by the definitions, rather than causes established by the group averages. For example, a checked account describing an interpretation problem would lead to a different follow-up from one describing a physical access barrier, even though both can receive the same accessibility label.
What might produce the group differences? Different services, exposure to several settings, different periods or expectations, and the amount people write are plausible explanations. The topic sample’s repeat contributors write somewhat longer texts; a separate length-mix check leaves the selected differences in the same direction. More than one explanation may contribute.
A profile’s activity over a long period cannot establish that its author is a caregiver, a frequent patient or someone following a referral pathway. The useful learning comes from validating what was described and connecting it to the hospital’s own evidence. Group patterns help select questions; they do not supply the answers on their own.

title: Whose Voices Shape Hospital Ratings
section: Recognize stable priorities and sensitive local scores
text:
Recognize stable priorities and sensitive local scores
The contributor differences leave the broad picture largely intact. Restricting the full text-review population to single-listing contributors changes the mean from 3.711 to 3.737 stars, or +0.025 before rounding. In the separate topic sample, the same top five topics remain in the same order: bedside manner, waiting, front desk, communication and nursing responsiveness. No topic moves more than one rank.
Those results support a stable broad agenda in this sample. Removing repeat contributors would reduce the available examples and modestly change topic prevalence, but does not substantially reorder the issues. Their share of the record also helps explain the small change in the pooled rating.

The contributor footprint

title: Whose Voices Shape Hospital Ratings
section: Use the findings for comparison and for improvement
text:
Use the findings for comparison and for improvement
For interpreting a score, start with a comparable context. Define the service, period and included feedback, then inspect local sensitivity and retained counts. If a conclusion changes with contributor composition, examine the accounts and relevant contextual evidence before making a performance claim. A filtered score is a diagnostic comparison, not automatically a better representation of experience.
For deciding what to investigate, start with the content. Keep the broad priorities in view, read relevant examples across rating bands and groups, and validate the particular problem before assigning follow-up. An accommodation barrier can deserve a response even when addressing it would barely change the star mean. The goal is a clearer understanding of the experience and an appropriate next step; this study has not evaluated the effect of an intervention.
For the next reporting discussion, bring one comparison whose population is explicit and one checked topic example with a defined follow-up question. The topic-pair analysis then extends the reading to issues people describe together.


Sources, comparison checks and original visualizations

Scope and groups. The collected record contains 3,138,214 reviews of 11,694 U.S. healthcare listings, including hospitals, emergency departments, clinics, medical centers and urgent care. The rating population uses 2,306,550 reviews with at least 15 characters of text and 2,173,013 contributor profiles. Groups count distinct Google listings per profile across the full observed period, 2007 to early June 2026. They do not measure repeat status at each past date, actual visits or physical institutions. Separate listings at one site can increase the count. Public feedback is self-selected. These calculated text-review means differ in scope from Google’s displayed rating, which can also include ratings without text.
The 11+ group. Its 46 profiles supply 964 text reviews and average 4.00 stars. The pooled all-profile mean includes this group; the single-only comparison removes both repeat groups. The listing-level histogram, direction counts and volume breakdown compare single-listing profiles with the combined single-plus-2–10 population and exclude 11+ from that baseline.
Decomposition and setting. The 8,707 listings with both main groups contribute to the within-listing and listing-mix components, weighted by repeat-profile review volume. Within-listing −0.061153, listing-mix −0.172939 and remainder −0.003177 sum to the −0.237269 pooled gap; listing mix accounts for 72.9%. These are arithmetic components, not causal mechanisms. The new setting table selects four Google categories with at least 20,000 eligible text reviews. Its group means are pooled within category, rather than adjusted within the same listings or matched services. Category and rating differences do not establish clinical quality or actual referral journeys.
Topic sample and validity. The separately drawn 2019+ sample contains 217,343 reviews; 196,183 distinct listing-plus-review keys pass the labeling analysis’s validity gates. The contributor-topic comparison narrows to 176,853 keys at 7,776 shared listings and excludes the 11+ group. Topic reach divides reviews mentioning a topic by labeled reviews in that contributor group. A review can mention multiple topics. Validity gates check permitted names, IDs, phrases, review resolution and known sentiment. They do not establish labeling accuracy. The 300-statement human audit remains unfinished; labels describe reported subjects, not verified events. The investigation questions above draw on full taxonomy definitions, not an inspection establishing which particular barrier explains the group gap.
Separate descriptive checks. The original topic chart pools rates across shared listings. The rating-band table compares 1–2 and 4–5 stars, with respective denominators of 55,673/9,838 and 92,968/13,449 single/repeat reviews. Mentions in those bands may have any sentiment. A separate standardization gives both groups identical listing weights, based on combined labeled-review volumes at each of the 7,776 listings. Equitable-treatment reach becomes 2.27%/3.03%, safety 3.95%/4.94%, and accessibility 0.93%/1.15% single/repeat. Equal-listing weights preserve the same directions. Another separate check standardizes the groups’ mix over four character-length bands: 15–99, 100–299, 300–999 and 1,000+. The selected directions persist. Median text lengths are 229/265 characters; mean distinct topics are 1.94/2.01. These checks assess particular compositional explanations separately. They do not jointly adjust listing, rating, date, service, text length and contributor characteristics, identify an intrinsic group trait, or establish statistical significance or causation.
Stable topic picture. Ranking all 29 topics by pooled reach before and after retaining single-listing profiles gives the same top five in the same order; the largest movement is one rank and Spearman correlation is 0.9985. For example, equitable-treatment reach changes from 2.368% to 2.223%, accessibility from 0.970% to 0.908%, and safety from 4.076% to 3.914%. Repeat contributors supply 13.7% of this sample, including 19.2% of accessibility, 18.9% of equitable-treatment and 17.1% of safety topic accounts. Those coverage shares do not establish that whole issues disappear, that information is unique to a group, or that every local service has the same priorities.
Local sensitivity and precision. The 6,224 eligible listings have at least 30 single-profile text contributions. The local shift equals the repeat share of single-plus-repeat contributions multiplied by the single-minus-repeat mean difference. This identity holds to numerical precision. Listing rank correlation is 0.998; the typical absolute shift is 0.030 stars. The preserved histogram uses shifts rounded to four decimals: 677 cross the 0.1-star boundary there, versus 674 using exact source means. Both are approximately 11%. The volume table and 45.6% share with lower single-only means use unrounded calculations. Neither the eligibility rule nor the marker validates a performance claim or determines whether feedback is important.
Preserved figures and evidence. All four original charts and the full topic table remain on this page. The earlier report retains detailed contributor distributions, geography, time and setting comparisons, 11+ profiles, and complete topic and sentiment plots. It is an exploratory archive; the interpretation here supersedes stronger claims there. Its time charts classify contributors using their final observed history, including later contributions. Download the original chart aggregates or expanded narrative evidence. The latter recomputes the source-based comparisons and retains their query definitions. All original group counts/means, decomposition components and 29 topic rates reconcile with the retained snapshots. No model is rerun, and no source text or contributor identifiers are exported.

title: Building a Topic Framework for Hospital Reviews
Building a Topic Framework for Hospital Reviews
section: Start with the accounts the vocabulary needs to describe
text:
Start with the accounts the vocabulary needs to describe
The source sample covers 10,029 U.S. healthcare listings, including hospitals, emergency departments, medical clinics, and urgent-care centers. “Hospital reviews” is shorthand for this broader collection. A vocabulary built from it needs room for appointment access and billing as well as experiences inside a hospital ward.
About 2.09 million text reviews were eligible. The selected sample covers 2019 to early June 2026, with sampling across years within each listing and a cap of 200 reviews per listing. That cap limits the influence of heavily reviewed locations. It does not make the sample representative of patients or care delivered across the United States.
The visual overview examines the rating distribution, geographic coverage, and care-setting differences in detail. Its maps remain interactive. Here, the key implication is narrower: the sample shapes which experiences the discovery process can find. An experience absent from these accounts cannot be recovered by consolidating their topic names.

title: Building a Topic Framework for Hospital Reviews
section: From 3,280 candidate names to 29 usable topics
text:
From 3,280 candidate names to 29 usable topics
Discovery worked in batches of up to 1,000 reviews. Rather than assign a fixed label to each review at this stage, the model proposed topics suggested by the batch. Across 216 usable outputs from 218 attempted batches, the run produced 3,280 topic candidates.
Those candidates were not 3,280 distinct kinds of experience. Separate batches can describe similar concerns with different names. Consolidation merged related candidates in two stages, first to 344 and then to 25 topics. A manual refinement pass brought the final vocabulary to 29.

The vocabulary is consolidated, then refined Each number counts topic candidates or definitions at that stage, rather than reviews. The steps are shown at equal size because they describe a process, not a scale.


3,280

Source: saved discovery report. The final increase reflects refinement, not an increase in the number of sampled reviews.

The staffing topic illustrates consolidation. Candidate names such as Staff shortages and understaffing and Understaffing and slow throughput became Staffing levels and operational capacity. Similar descriptions could now be counted together.
The final refinement made selected topics more specific. Twenty-one topics remained; four broad topics were replaced by eight narrower ones:







Before refinement
Distinctions in the final framework




Staff interaction and bedside manner
Front-desk conduct; clinical bedside manner


Billing, insurance, and financial aspects
Billing and charges; insurance coverage and denials


Facility environment, comfort, and amenities
Facility condition and comfort; food, parking, and amenities


Medication and pain management
Medication and pharmacy; pain management



A disputed charge and a coverage denial may require different records and expertise. A prescription delay raises a different question from pain not being taken seriously. Preserving those distinctions gives a team a more useful starting point than a broad “financial” or “medication” score.
Discovery counts alone cannot tell us how common any of these experiences are. A candidate can recur across batches or overlap another candidate. For that, we need the separate labeling pass that applies the final definitions to individual reviews.

title: Building a Topic Framework for Hospital Reviews
section: What a single “staff” score would hide
text:
What a single “staff” score would hide
Applying the framework makes the reason for these distinctions concrete. Clinical bedside manner appears in 41.7% of labeled reviews, front-desk conduct in 25.3%, and nursing responsiveness in 11.8%. Their tone differs too: about 21%, 37%, and 41% of their positive-or-negative statements are negative, respectively.
Praise for clinical interactions can therefore coexist with a less favorable picture of administrative contact or practical assistance. For a patient-experience team, that suggests separate questions: what do reviewers value in clinical interactions, what happens at reception, and what do accounts of requests for help describe?
Switch between staff feedback and cleanliness/protective practices to compare the selected topics on a common scale. These model-derived estimates describe sampled public feedback and remain provisional pending human validation.

title: Building a Topic Framework for Hospital Reviews
section: Clear boundaries matter more than a neat topic count
text:
Clear boundaries matter more than a neat topic count
Consolidation is not just a naming exercise. Merge too much and “communication” could absorb every problem involving an interaction. Split too much and closely related accounts could be scattered across near-duplicate topics. The useful test is whether the definitions preserve a distinction a reader can understand and a labeler can apply.
The examples below illustrate where that judgment enters. They are invented examples for explaining the definitions, not quotations or additional findings. The suggested topics are a reading of the current definitions, not audited model outputs.


Code
boundaryExamples = ([
  {name:"Waiting or communication?",first:"The appointment began two hours late.",firstTopic:"Wait times and timeliness of care",second:"Nobody explained why the appointment was delayed.",secondTopic:"Communication and information sharing",explanation:"The first statement describes elapsed time; the second describes missing information. A review containing both can support both topics. A delay alone does not establish a communication failure."},
  {name:"Bedside manner or nursing responsiveness?",first:"The nurse listened carefully and treated me with respect.",firstTopic:"Clinical staff bedside manner and empathy",second:"I pressed the call button repeatedly before someone helped me to the bathroom.",secondTopic:"Nursing responsiveness and basic care needs",explanation:"Both statements concern nursing, but they describe different experiences: the manner of an interaction and the response to a practical care need. The staff member's role alone does not determine the topic."},
  {name:"Billing or insurance?",first:"The bill charged me twice for the same test.",firstTopic:"Billing, charges and collections",second:"My insurer denied coverage for the test.",secondTopic:"Insurance coverage, denials and network issues",explanation:"One statement disputes a charge; the other concerns coverage. An unexpected bill with no further explanation may not establish which problem occurred. The label should follow what the account actually says."},
  {name:"Cleanliness or infection control?",first:"The bathroom floor was dirty.",firstTopic:"Cleanliness and housekeeping",second:"Staff did not follow the posted isolation precautions.",secondTopic:"Infection control and health safety practices",explanation:"The distinction is between the condition of the space and a described safety practice. Neither statement, by itself, proves that an infection occurred."}
])








Where would you draw the boundary?


Code
viewof chosenBoundary = themedSelect(boundaryExamples.map(d=>d.name),{label:"Compare topics"})









Code
boundary = boundaryExamples.find(d=>d.name===chosenBoundary)









Code
html`<div class="taxonomy-boundary" aria-live="polite"><p class="taxonomy-count">Invented examples · illustrative assignments</p><dl><div><dt>${boundary.first}</dt><dd>Suggested topic: ${boundary.firstTopic}</dd></div><div><dt>${boundary.second}</dt><dd>Suggested topic: ${boundary.secondTopic}</dd></div></dl><p>${boundary.explanation}</p></div>`








These examples also expose a limit of short definitions. Real accounts can sit between topics: a sentence about delayed test results may involve both diagnostic services and communication. The wording, the surrounding account, and consistent labeling rules matter. A human audit needs to examine those cases, not just confirm that the chosen topic exists in the list.
Some boundaries remain imperfect. The full facility-condition definition explicitly overlaps cleanliness, although the short explorer description makes that less apparent. A usable framework needs rules for such cases and checks of how labels are applied.
Different follow-up needs can also justify a distinction when the tone is similar. Medication/pharmacy and pain-management statements are about 73% and 74% negative, respectively. A refill problem and an account of inadequate pain relief still raise different questions. A large sentiment difference is one way to demonstrate a topic boundary’s value; it is not the only test.

title: Building a Topic Framework for Hospital Reviews
section: From a label to a follow-up question
text:
From a label to a follow-up question
For a hospital team, the framework is most useful when a topic leads to a specific question and the appropriate people to examine it. These are possible uses, to adapt to the hospital’s organization:







Feedback distinction
A concrete follow-up




Front-desk conduct vs clinical bedside manner
With registration and patient-experience teams, read whether reception accounts concern courtesy, unanswered questions, or difficulty completing an administrative task. Retain what reviewers value in clinical interactions.


Clinical manner vs nursing responsiveness
With the relevant nursing or service lead, inspect accounts of requests for practical help separately from descriptions of warmth and respect. Check service context and available response records.


Billing vs insurance
With billing and coverage/authorization teams, distinguish disputed charges, coverage decisions, and explanation gaps. Read connected accounts together before deciding which process to investigate.


Cleanliness vs protective practices
With housekeeping and infection-prevention leads, distinguish the condition of a space from a described practice. Verify the accounts through the hospital’s existing processes.



Check the accounts, identify the process, and compare the feedback with the hospital’s own evidence. These follow-ups are proposed applications of the framework, rather than interventions tested by this study. The analysis cannot tell us which change would improve care or how many stars it would gain.
The hospital overview shows how frequently topics appear and how their tone differs. The later articles examine repeat reviewers, topics worth reading together, and associations with star ratings. The shared vocabulary gives those analyses a way to move from a broad rating to a focused question. Its usefulness depends on preserving relevant distinctions and applying them reliably; 29 is the result of this process, rather than a uniquely correct number of topics.


Method details, source material, and preserved visualizations

Sampling. The saved report records a minimum of 20 reviews per eligible source listing, a maximum of 200 selected reviews per listing, year-stratified sampling, and random seed 42. The 20-review minimum is an eligibility rule, not a guarantee of 20 sampled reviews per listing. The coverage sample includes 217,343 reviews; 217,135 are matched to a U.S. state and 208 are not. Collection ends in early June 2026.
Discovery and consolidation. The report lists GPT-5.4 nano for discovery, batches of up to 1,000 reviews, and DeepSeek V4 Pro for consolidation. Of 218 attempted discovery batches, 216 produced usable outputs. The summary does not establish which experiences might have been lost from the other two. Manual refinement follows the automated 25-topic result; it is distinct from auditing the labels later assigned to reviews.
Source trail. Discovery counts, topic names, short descriptions, and category membership come from the retained report. Comparing the saved 25-topic consolidation with the 29-topic final vocabulary establishes the four refinements shown above. The staffing-name example is documented in the source project’s notebooks/hospitals_topic_labeling/build_notebook.py. The four boundary comparisons are newly written illustrations. Download the explorer data or the full frozen catalog; the existing extraction script preserves the explorer’s descriptions without rerunning a model.
Measured examples. The later labeling pass retains 425,667 statements across 196,183 distinct listing-and-review keys after checks of topic name, topic ID, quoted phrase, review resolution, and known sentiment. Reach counts each review once per topic. Negative share is negative ÷ (negative + positive) statements. The new comparison reuses the overview’s saved aggregates, independently recomputed from the original label file for all 29 topics. Medication and pain figures come from the same checked aggregates. These checks confirm the calculations and mechanical validity, not human agreement with every label. The 300-statement human audit remains unfinished. Download the five chart examples.
All original visuals remain available. The original exploratory report retains the interactive coverage map, ratings and annual sample counts, listing mix and category breadth, topic explorer, and discovery examples. The overview carries the coverage map into the site’s current design. Interpretations here supersede the earlier report’s stronger claims about what the taxonomy establishes; its shortened snippets should not be treated as a new set of verified quotations.

The shuffled list contained the same 23 topic definitions, but in a different order on each request. It produced just one 256-token cache hit across all 20 batches. Keeping the meaning unchanged was insufficient; the sequence of repeated content mattered too.
Output lengths varied slightly between runs, so the difference between their total bills is not a perfectly isolated measure of the cache discount. The chart’s ticks provide that separate comparison: they hold each run’s input and output token counts fixed and price all input as uncached. For the layout with metadata after the static block, that calculation is $35.32 without caching versus $25.84 with the recorded cache hits.

title: Reducing LLM Costs with Prompt Caching
section: What the cache reuses
text:
What the cache reuses
The prefix is the beginning of a request. When successive requests start with the same content, prefix caching can reuse processing associated with that shared beginning. A changing field placed early can interrupt the match before the instructions or topic list are reached.
For this labeling task, the request can be understood as two blocks:
UNCHANGED BETWEEN REQUESTS
  System instructions
  Labeling rules
  Fixed topic list, in a fixed order
  Required response format

CHANGING BETWEEN REQUESTS
  Batch identifier, if needed
  Ten new customer reviews
The cache does not supply a saved answer for the new reviews. The model still generates their labels, and output tokens are billed separately. The API reports reused input as prompt_cache_hit_tokens and the remaining input as prompt_cache_miss_tokens.
At the prices saved for this experiment, a million cached input tokens cost $0.0028, compared with $0.14 for uncached input: a 50-fold difference. That explains how a moderately longer request could be cheaper if enough of it was reused. The complete rates and cost calculation are retained in the methods note below; the provider’s pricing page lists current rates.

What happened during warm-up
In the static-first run, the first two requests received no cache hits. Every request from batch 3 onward reported exactly 768 cached input tokens. The remaining input varied because each batch contained different reviews.

In this run, reuse began on the third request Cache-friendly production layout, one bar per request of 10 reviews. The first two calls miss; from batch 3 onward exactly 768 input tokens are served from cache.

This is the warm-up pattern we observed, not a promise that caching always starts on the third request. Cache availability is best-effort provider behavior; the DeepSeek caching guide describes the feature.
Two measurements help separate cost from behavior. The overall cached share includes every request, including warm-up, and is the percentage used in the opening table. The steady-state measurements exclude the first three requests so we can inspect reuse after warm-up. In this run, 48.8% of all input was cached; after excluding those requests, the share was 53.3%. These are shares of input tokens, not percentages of requests that received a hit.

section: Why a shorter prompt can cost more

Why a shorter prompt can cost more
An earlier experiment exposed the problem while we were trying to shorten the prompt. One version kept complete topic and category names. A second shortened JSON field names (for example, topic_id became t) while retaining the descriptive values. A third removed repeated category names and used short topic codes that Python mapped back to the full hierarchy afterward.
The difference is illustrated by a topic such as staff friendliness. Shortening a field name leaves “Service” and “Staff friendliness” in the prompt. The more aggressive version keeps the topic description but replaces its place in the hierarchy with a code. Both reduce text, but they change different parts of the repeated setup.

Shorter field names worked better in this comparison: they reduced tokens while retaining cache reuse. That is an observed result for these prompts, rather than a guarantee that one representation will always be cheaper.
The experiment changed several aspects of the request, including its length, representation, and, in additional variants, schema placement. It revealed the tradeoff but did not isolate why a particular version stopped receiving hits. The two diagnostic experiments below were designed to examine that behavior more directly.

title: Reducing LLM Costs with Prompt Caching
section: What determines how much input gets reused?
text:
What determines how much input gets reused?
The production layouts showed the cost difference. Two smaller diagnostic tests examined the amount of unchanged content and the position of the first changing field. Each configuration used 20 batches of ten reviews with reasoning disabled; the charts report median cached tokens after excluding the first three batches.

How much unchanged content comes first?
The first test began with a minimal one-topic prompt and added increasing amounts of identical filler text before the reviews. This artificial setup made it possible to explore short prefixes; the full production prompt was already long enough to receive hits.
Without padding, the prompt received no hits in 20 requests. The first padded setting, targeting 128 added tokens, received 256 cached tokens on every one of the 17 steady-state requests. The total reusable beginning included the instructions as well as the added padding, which is why those two numbers differ.

More unchanged content made more input available for reuse A minimal prompt received increasing amounts of identical filler text. The horizontal axis counts added padding, not the complete prompt prefix. Dots show tested settings; the line connects them.

  ...chartBase(320),

  y: {label: "Cached tokens per request after warm-up", grid: true, ticks: [0, 512, 1024, 1536, 2048], tickFormat: fmt},
  marks: [
    Plot.rectX([0], {x1: 0, x2: 128, y1: 0, y2: 2200, fill: C.panel}),
    Plot.lineY(threshold, {x: "pad", y: "steady_hit_tokens", stroke: C.accent, strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.dot(threshold, {x: "pad", y: "steady_hit_tokens", fill: C.accent, r: 3.5, tip: {format: {x: fmt, y: fmt}}}),
    Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: C.ink})

Source: cache_threshold_summary.csv. Cached tokens are medians over batches 4–20.

All the padded settings received hits on every steady-state request. As padding increased, the amount reused generally increased too. The higher cached share did not mean hits were becoming more reliable; more of each request was simply unchanged text.
This experiment does not establish that adding filler saves money. It measured reuse, and extra padding still has a cost. For an actual labeling job, the useful action is to preserve the instructions and reference material already needed, then measure the bill.


Where does the first changing field appear?
The second test kept a large prompt fixed and inserted a line containing the changing batch number at different positions. If that line appeared within the first 192 words, the API reported no cache hits. Placing it later preserved more reuse: at the tested positions of 256, 1,024, and 2,048 words, the median reported hits were 256, 1,024, and 2,048 tokens respectively. Without the inserted field, the median was 3,328 tokens.

Source: cache_breaker_position_summary.csv; first 3 batches excluded from steady metrics.

Here the insertion positions are measured in words, while the API reports reuse in tokens. The numerical matches at those settings are specific to the test text; words and tokens are not interchangeable units. The practical result is that moving the changing field later left more of the beginning available for reuse. Identical text after that field did not restore the lost benefit.
Across both scans, the smallest nonzero reported hit was 256 tokens and every nonzero hit count was a multiple of 128. Those observations are consistent with reuse in discrete units, but they do not establish a universal 256-token minimum or uniquely identify a 128-token cache implementation. They describe this model and workload on the experiment date.

title: Reducing LLM Costs with Prompt Caching
section: A prompt layout to use and verify
text:
A prompt layout to use and verify
For this workload, a useful starting layout is:
Fixed instructions → fixed topic list → fixed response format → changing metadata → new reviews.
The batch-identifier example shows why the boundary matters. A field can be useful for tracking requests without occupying the first line. Likewise, a topic list can retain its meaning while changing its order, but that change may prevent reuse.
When building or revising a labeling prompt:

Keep repeated content consistent. Use the same topic order, section names, and formatting between requests.
Place changing fields after the reusable block. Check batch identifiers, timestamps, and other per-request metadata as well as the review text.
Measure after a change. Inspect cache-hit and cache-miss tokens, output tokens, and total cost; a shorter prompt or a higher cached percentage alone does not establish a saving.
Check representative requests after warm-up. Inspect several batches to understand reuse, while including the initial requests in the total bill.

These tests measured cache behavior and cost, not labeling quality or latency. A prompt change still needs to produce useful labels. The result worth carrying into another workload is the testable layout principle: keep the necessary repeated content together at the beginning, then verify what the provider actually reuses.


Methods, historical pricing, and sources

Scope. The controlled experiments used deepseek-v4-flash on May 31, 2026, with reasoning disabled and 200 reviews per configuration. Production validation used the fixed 23-topic taxonomy; the padding test used a minimal one-topic prompt. The earlier format comparison used 1,000 reviews per variant with reasoning enabled. All used ten reviews per batch. A run-specific identifier in the system message was held constant within each controlled run and changed between runs to separate their cache prefixes.
Historical rates. The saved cost rollup used the following prices, recorded on May 31, 2026. These are experiment inputs, not current pricing. Model versions, rates, and caching behavior can change.

title: From 113,518 Reviews to 23 Topics
From 113,518 Reviews to 23 Topics
section: Why the topic list comes first
text:
Why the topic list comes first
We started with 113,518 cleaned customer reviews of electricians, plumbers, roofers, and other local tradespeople in Lower Saxony, Germany. We wanted to understand what customers discussed across these businesses. Before we could count mentions of pricing, punctuality, or workmanship, we needed a consistent list of topics.
Choosing that list ourselves would be straightforward, but it could miss concerns we had not anticipated. Asking a language model to invent labels independently for every review creates a different problem: similar concerns receive different names. “Punctuality,” “Keeping appointments,” and “Arriving on time” might become three labels even when they describe the same customer experience. Counting them separately would fragment the result.
An analyst could instead define topics and write keyword rules for each one. That can work well for known questions, but discovering unexpected concerns still requires looking beyond the topics already on the list.
We therefore separated discovery from labeling. First, we used a sample of 30,000 reviews to identify candidate topics. Then we consolidated those candidates into 23 topics, organized into ten groups. The aim was a manageable list that an analyst could review before using it to label individual reviews across the corpus.

title: From 113,518 Reviews to 23 Topics
section: The workflow at a glance
text:
The workflow at a glance
A taxonomy is simply the agreed list of topics and how they are grouped. In this workflow, the topic names emerge from the review text; we do not supply a predefined list. We do give the model context about the businesses and a target range for the number of topics, so the result is guided by both the data and our instructions.


01 Prepare the reviews
113,518 cleaned reviews
sample 30,000 reviews


02 Discover candidate topics
414 candidate entries
30,000 reviews in 30 batches
gpt-5.4-nano
retain names and supporting phrases


03 Consolidate overlapping topics
23 topics
proposed in one global pass
deepseek-v4-pro
group the topics for analysis


04 Organize and review
10 groups
Check definitions and assignments before labeling


Discovery ran in 30 batches of 1,000 reviews. Each batch was processed independently, producing a total of 414 candidate topic entries. These were not 414 distinct customer concerns: many entries described similar things in different words. Consolidation compared those suggestions together and produced the 23-topic list.
The two stages used different models. A small model, gpt-5.4-nano, handled batch discovery; deepseek-v4-pro handled consolidation and grouping. The reasoning behind this division was to keep repeated discovery calls inexpensive while using a more capable model for decisions about which topics belong together. These were the models used in this run, not a benchmark of the best models for the task.
Scroll on to follow the reviews through the pipeline.

        0523 topics in 10 groupsThe result is a list an analyst can read, question, and edit before any review is labeled. Only then does counting start.

text:
Discover topics and keep the evidence
For each batch, the model proposes topics and includes short phrases from the reviews to support them. We retain both: the name describes the concern, while the phrases let us inspect what the model meant. A label such as “reliability” is easier to interpret when we can see whether its examples concern appointments, emergency help, or keeping promises more generally.
The excerpts below illustrate the kind of evidence carried through the workflow. The English translations and concern labels are included here to help explain them.

These are short excerpts from the discovery artifacts, selected for publication without names, businesses, or places. The translations are explanatory; the original phrases remain the evidence.

Because batches are processed independently, the same concern can appear repeatedly under different names. One batch might suggest “Punctuality and meeting deadlines,” another “Punctual appointments and schedule adherence.” At this stage, we keep those overlapping suggestions so that consolidation can compare their meanings and supporting phrases.
This repetition gives recurring concerns several opportunities to surface. It does not guarantee that we find every important issue, but it gives us more evidence to inspect than a single topic name would provide.

Several candidate entries can feed one final topic. Mapped candidate entries per topic, not the number of reviews mentioning it. Hover a dot to see its group.

title: From 113,518 Reviews to 23 Topics
section: Turn overlapping topics into a consistent vocabulary
text:
Turn overlapping topics into a consistent vocabulary
Consolidation turns the batch outputs into a list that can be used consistently. To see what this involves, consider an illustrative grouping of suggestions about scheduling:








Candidate suggestions
Proposed final topic
Reason for grouping




Punctuality and meeting deadlines; punctual appointments and schedule adherence; reliable scheduling
Appointment scheduling, punctuality, and timely completion
They concern arranging appointments, keeping agreed times, and completing work on schedule.


Fast emergency help; rapid response to a breakdown
Emergency and rapid response
They concern availability and speed when something urgent goes wrong.



Both topics concern time, but they answer different questions. “Did the electrician arrive at the agreed time?” is different from “Could someone come immediately when the heating failed?” Keeping that distinction makes the result more useful than a broad label such as “speed.” The table illustrates the decision; the full saved names appear in the taxonomy below.
In our run, the consolidation model received all 414 candidate entries and their supporting phrases in one call. This lets it compare possible groupings across the whole set. With a long chain of pairwise merges, an early grouping can become progressively broader as later topics are added. Considering the set together avoids that particular sequence of decisions, although it still leaves room for mistakes.
We use three rules to guide the grouping:

Compare meanings and evidence together. Similar names are a starting point, but the review phrases help establish whether the suggestions concern the same experience.
Give each candidate entry one explicit assignment. This makes omissions and duplicate assignments checkable. The final definitions should also explain where neighboring topics differ; an instruction to avoid overlap is not enough on its own.
Keep the subject separate from the opinion. “Fair pricing” and “overpriced” express different opinions about the same subject. Both belong under pricing; their sentiment can be recorded separately during labeling.

The one-assignment rule applies to the candidate entries being consolidated. It does not mean that an individual review can discuss only one topic.

title: From 113,518 Reviews to 23 Topics
section: Review the taxonomy before using it

title: From 113,518 Reviews to 23 Topics
section: What this approach can and cannot tell you
text:
What this approach can and cannot tell you
The workflow produces a topic list supported by review examples. It does not establish that the list is exhaustive, that every grouping is correct, or how frequently each concern occurs. Three boundaries matter when using the result:

The aim is to miss as few relevant concerns as possible. We processed a sample of 30,000 reviews in independent batches and retained supporting phrases so the proposed topics could be checked. This approach aims to capture a broad range of concerns while keeping discovery manageable. Uncommon concerns may still need targeted sampling, and consolidation needs review to ensure they remain visible.
The saved output still needs an assignment check. This run contains 409 mapped candidate references out of 414. Five entries remain unaccounted for in the mapping and need review before it can be treated as complete. That does not establish that five distinct concerns are missing, but it shows why model instructions need to be followed by validation.
Discovery counts are not review frequencies. A topic suggested repeatedly across batches is not automatically the most prevalent topic. Measuring prevalence requires applying the agreed list to individual reviews and defining how those labels will be counted.

The same sequence can be adapted to restaurant reviews, support tickets, or survey responses, with domain context and sampling suited to each source. In each case, the useful deliverable is a topic list that people can inspect, refine, and then apply consistently.
Once that review is complete, the next step is to label individual reviews and measure which topics appear. The companion article, “Reading 200,000 Reviews with LLMs: Without Overpaying”, examines how to carry out that labeling step economically.

title: Reading Customer Opinions at Scale
text:
Star ratings and survey scores tell you how customers feel on average. The text they write tells you what happened, in their own words. This article explains why that text is worth analyzing, where it adds value, and how the ways of reading it at scale have changed.
A four-star review of a heating repair can contain praise for a friendly technician, a complaint about a late arrival, and a surprise on the invoice. The rating compresses all three into one number. The text keeps them apart.
That difference is the starting point for everything on this site. We test methods for turning large volumes of customer text into evidence that can be counted, checked, and traced back to what people actually wrote. Before the individual experiments, it helps to see the landscape: what text adds, where it is used, which families of methods exist, and why none of them removes the need to validate the result.

title: Reading Customer Opinions at Scale
section: Why read what customers write
text:
Why read what customers write
Structured measures ask customers to answer questions someone chose in advance. Text works the other way round. Customers decide what to mention, and they describe it in their own terms. That makes it possible to find issues nobody thought to ask about.
Text analysis sits between qualitative and quantitative research. It keeps some of the depth of reading individual accounts while reaching the scale of a survey. A widely cited review in the Journal of Marketing describes a simple sequence that still holds: prepare the text, analyze it, turn the result into measures, and validate those measures before using them.
Text also has limits. People who write reviews choose to do so, and they choose what to write about. Text shows what customers say, not necessarily what most customers experience.

title: Reading Customer Opinions at Scale
section: What text has revealed in research
text:
What text has revealed in research
Research has shown repeatedly that text carries information the usual numbers miss.

Market structure without a survey. Mining car and health forums produced maps of which products consumers compare. They matched brand-switching data closely, and the same approach surfaced drug side effects that a major health reference did not list (Marketing Science, 2012).
Signals that financial data misses. In peer-to-peer lending, the text of loan applications helped predict default beyond the financial information.
Ratings hide more than text. Across many review platforms, star ratings are polarized by who chooses to write, while the review text is less extreme. An average rating can conceal what the text still says.

title: Reading Customer Opinions at Scale

text:
Where the analysis creates value
Text analysis is rarely the end product. Its value comes from feeding familiar marketing and customer decisions with evidence that numbers alone do not provide.

Methods that learn from examples read context but need those examples. Methods that discover structure need interpretation. Language models combine several of these strengths and add new costs and risks.

Measuring well-defined constructs

Often the most accurate for a fixed task
Needs training data; categories are fixed
High-volume, stable classification


Topic models (LDA, BERTopic)
The number of topics, roughly

Two points from the research behind this table are worth keeping in mind. Trained models usually beat word lists on accuracy, and in sentiment analysis the difference can be large enough to change the conclusions drawn. Topic models, on the other hand, discover themes but do not name them: the statistically best model is not always the one people find easiest to interpret.

title: Reading Customer Opinions at Scale
section: What language models change, and what they do not
text:
What language models change, and what they do not
Large language models changed three practical things.
First, categories no longer need training data. A model can be given a list of topics and asked to apply them, or asked to propose topics from the text itself. Prompt-based approaches such as TopicGPT generate topic descriptions and then assign documents to them.
Second, outputs can be read directly. Instead of a list of words, a model can return a named topic, a sentiment, and the phrase that supports the label. That evidence makes individual assignments easy to inspect.
Third, annotation became cheap enough to test at scale. Language models have proved competitive with crowd workers on several annotation tasks, and marketing research is testing where they can support parts of human analysis.
Other things did not change. Customers who write reviews are still a self-selected group, and associations in text are still associations, not causes. Some problems are new:

Results can vary. Small changes in wording, or simply running the same input again, can change a model’s output.
Models change or disappear. Hosted models can be updated or retired, which makes exact replication difficult.
Benchmarks can be contaminated. If test data appeared in a model’s training data, reported accuracy can be too optimistic.
Cost scales with volume. Every review sent to a hosted model has a price, and how the prompt is structured can change it considerably.
Summaries can drop small groups. A fluent overview of thousands of comments can leave out issues raised by only a few people.

title: Reading Customer Opinions at Scale
section: The rule that does not change: validate
text:
The rule that does not change: validate
Every approach above produces numbers that look precise. Whether they measure what they claim to measure is a separate question, and it has to be answered with evidence rather than assumed.


01 Define what counts Write down the categories and what belongs in each before looking at results. apply to a sample


02 Compare with people Check model labels against human coders on examples the method has not seen. measure agreement


03 Look at rare categories Make sure small categories have enough examples to be checked at all. freeze the setup


04 Record the setup Keep the model, prompt, and settings so the result can be reproduced.


A clear prompt is not the same thing as a valid measure. Comparison with human judgment remains the standard, including for the small categories that are easiest to overlook.

title: Reading Customer Opinions at Scale
section: What the articles on this site test
text:
What the articles on this site test
The articles here take the language-model approach and examine it piece by piece, using recorded runs rather than impressions.

From 113,518 Reviews to 23 Topics shows how a topic list can be discovered from the reviews themselves and reviewed before use.
Reading 200,000 Reviews with LLMs: Without Overpaying measures what output format, reasoning settings, caching, and batch size do to the cost of labeling.
Reducing LLM Costs with Prompt Caching shows why the order of a prompt can change the bill for the same work.
What LLM Summaries Miss in Customer Feedback tests how often summaries lose rare topics compared with labeling each document.

The analyses apply the same methods to a single question.

The example review was written for illustration and does not come from any dataset.

title: Reading 200,000 Reviews with LLMs: Without Overpaying
Reading 200,000 Reviews with LLMs: Without Overpaying
section: From customer reviews to usable labels
text:
From customer reviews to usable labels
We wanted to turn roughly 200,000 German reviews of local tradespeople into a dataset we could analyze. For each relevant passage, a language model assigned a topic, recorded its sentiment, and copied the phrase that supported the label.
At that scale, keeping the API bill low was part of the task. For a fixed model and token prices, cost grows with the input and output tokens used: every request sends instructions and reviews, and every extracted label adds output. We therefore asked which parts of that usage we could reduce: the input tokens per review, the output tokens per label, and the repeated instructions across requests. We also tested caching to make repeated input cheaper. The aim was to lower the cost while retaining labels useful for the analysis.
We then compared different configurations on the same 1,000-review sample. Shorter outputs, disabled reasoning, prompt caching, and larger batches brought the estimated API cost down to about $15 per million reviews. This article explains which changes made the difference and what we checked before deciding whether the cheaper configuration was useful.
The model receives instructions, a fixed list of 23 topics, and a batch of reviews. It returns a set of labels that can be stored and counted. The topic list comes from a separate discovery step, described in “From 113,518 Reviews to 23 Topics”.


01 Select and batch reviews
Choose the records needed for the analysis and split them into batches.
reviews to label


02 Build the prompt
Keep instructions and the 23-topic list first; put the review batch last.
send to the model


03 Extract labels
Return each review ID, copied phrase, topic code, and sentiment.
structured output


04 Store the results
Look up full topic names and keep the labels linked to their source reviews.


The easiest way to see what labeling produces is to follow a single review through it. Scroll through the steps below.

  
    
      
        
          ★★★★★Heating repair · illustrative review
          Called on Monday because our heating had failed1, and they came the very next morning2. The technician was friendly3 and explained what was wrong4. He left everything clean and tidy5. Only the invoice was higher than the quote, and nobody could explain why6.
        
        
          1Heating system installations, repairs, and maintenanceneutral
          2Emergency and rapid responsepositive
          3Staff friendliness and courtesypositive
          4Professional consultation and advicepositive
          5Workmanship cleanliness and site tidinesspositive
          6Pricing transparency and value for moneynegative
        
      

      
        Review R0417 · six labels
        “our heating had failed”Heating system installations, repairs, and maintenanceneutral✓
        “they came the very next morning”Emergency and rapid responsepositive✓
        “The technician was friendly”Staff friendliness and courtesypositive✓
        “explained what was wrong”Professional consultation and advicepositive✓
        “He left everything clean and tidy”Workmanship cleanliness and site tidinesspositive✓
        “the invoice was higher than the quote, and nobody could explain why”Pricing transparency and value for moneynegative✓
        ✓ phrase found word for word in the review
      

      
        
        Illustration, not measured counts. Grey marks stand for labels from other reviews. Filled endpoints are this review's six labels; hollow endpoints mean it adds no label to that topic.
      
    
  

  
    Start with one review. This one is written for illustration and shown in English; the reviews in the study were German. In a few sentences it covers timing, staff, advice, tidiness, and price.
    Find what is said, not the overall mood. The model looks for passages that make a specific point and copies each one exactly as written.
    Match each passage to a topic. Every passage gets one of the 23 topics from the fixed list. A single review can receive several labels, here six.
    Add a sentiment to each label. Four labels are positive, one is neutral, and one is negative. The four-star rating alone would hide the complaint about the invoice.
    Store the labels as data. Each row keeps the review ID, the copied phrase, the topic, and the sentiment. Because the phrase is copied word for word, we can check it against the review automatically. That check is the exact-phrase match rate used later in this article.
    Only then count. Each label adds one mark to its topic. Across roughly 200,000 reviews these marks become the topic counts, and every count can still be traced back to the phrases behind it.
  


Keeping the original phrase with each label makes it possible to inspect what the model extracted, rather than relying on a topic count alone.

title: Reading 200,000 Reviews with LLMs: Without Overpaying
section: Establish a baseline on the same workload
text:
Establish a baseline on the same workload
The main experiment used deepseek-v4-flash, the fixed taxonomy, and the same 1,000-review slice. We varied the output format, reasoning setting, and batch size, recording token usage and checking the returned labels. Holding the review sample constant made the configurations easier to compare.
Costs below are estimates per million reviews, calculated from those small runs using the token prices applied to the experiment on May 30, 2026: $0.0028 per million cached input tokens, $0.14 per million uncached input tokens, and $0.28 per million output tokens. They describe provider API charges, not the cost of data collection, engineering, or human review.
The verbose batch-10 run cost approximately $104 per million reviews with its recorded cache hits. Pricing exactly the same token usage as if every input token missed the cache gives a $129 reference baseline. This second number is a calculation, not a separate observed run.
We tracked two kinds of result:







Measure
What it tells us




Estimated API cost
How recorded input, output, and cache usage translate into a bill.


Exact-phrase match rate
The share of returned label phrases that appear verbatim in their source review.


Labeling rate and label count
How many reviews receive any label, and how many labels the model emits.


Distinct topics emitted
How many of the 23 allowed topics appear at least once in the output.



The output checks describe copying fidelity and labeling behavior. They do not, by themselves, establish whether the topics or sentiments are correct. We return to that distinction when comparing the baseline with the optimized result.
Other exploratory runs used OpenAI models on different review slices. Those comparisons need matched inputs before they can support a model ranking; the savings described here come from changing the configuration of the same DeepSeek model.

section: Reduce the cost of the model’s answer
text:
Reduce the cost of the model’s answer
Language models charge for both the text they receive and the tokens they generate. In the uncached reference calculation, output accounted for about 80% of the bill. That made the answer an important place to look for savings.

Output accounted for about 80% of the uncached reference cost. Cost per 1M reviews for the verbose, batch-10 run priced without any cache hits: output is about 80% of the total.

Test whether reasoning helps this task

The reasoning-disabled configurations used roughly 70% fewer output tokens in these pairs and had higher exact-phrase match rates. That supports testing this setting for a similar extraction task. It does not tell us that reasoning is unnecessary for every labeling problem, or that the cheaper output has identical topic and sentiment accuracy.


Return codes instead of repeating names
The other source of avoidable output was information already available in the topic list. A verbose label repeated the full topic name and its broader category for every extracted phrase.
The following illustrative outputs represent the same label. In the compact version, the application can recover the topic and category names by looking up T003.

→


Compact output
{
  "i": "I001",
  "p": "freundliche Mitarbeiter",
  "t": "T003",
  "s": "positive"

The key legend is defined once in the instructions: i is the review ID, p the copied phrase, t the topic code, and s the sentiment. The phrase remains unchanged; only the representation becomes smaller.
With reasoning enabled and ten reviews per request, switching from verbose labels to compact codes reduced estimated cost from $104.19 to $97.64 per million reviews. Both configurations emitted 22 of the 23 topics. The saving was smaller than the reduction from disabling reasoning, but it removed repeated text that the application could supply through a lookup.

title: Reading 200,000 Reviews with LLMs: Without Overpaying
section: Reuse the prompt and batch reviews efficiently
text:
Reuse the prompt and batch reviews efficiently
Every request includes instructions and the topic list, even though only the reviews change. Caching can reduce the price of that repeated input; batching spreads the repeated material across more reviews.

Keep the reusable prompt first
A provider-side prompt cache can reuse a previously processed prefix. To make that possible, keep the instructions and topic list stable and put changing content after them:



Reusable beginning
Changing content at the end




Instructions → topic list
Batch metadata → reviews



Use the same topic order and serialization on each call. A changing identifier or timestamp placed before the topic list can prevent reuse of that part of the prompt. Stable layout supports caching, but cache hits are best-effort behavior and should be checked in the provider’s returned usage fields.

Recorded cache hits lowered the reference run’s estimated cost. The same token usage priced with observed cache hits ($104.19) and with all input billed as a miss ($129.11), per million reviews.

The whole job did not become 50 times cheaper: output still had to be generated, and the changing review text still incurred input cost. For this run, recorded cache hits reduced the estimated bill from the $129.11 no-cache reference to $104.19, about 19%.
The separate article “Reducing LLM Costs with Prompt Caching” tests prompt layout directly. Here, the chart compares two prices for the same recorded token usage.
