section: Reduce the workload without changing the question
text:
Reduce the workload without changing the question
The previous changes lowered cost per review. A separate decision is how many reviews the analysis needs and which model calls can be reused.
Date filtering defines the population being analyzed. Of 197,827 eligible reviews, 100,611 were dated from 2023 through 2026. Restricting the analysis to that period removed about 49% of the workload. That is useful for a question about recent customer experience, but it would exclude information needed for a longer historical comparison.
Duplicate handling can avoid repeated model calls. When identical text is labeled under the same instructions and context, the result can be reused. Attach those labels back to every original record so that review counts and business-level analysis retain their meaning. Repeated phrases such as “Sehr gut” (“Very good”) still represent separate customer reviews, even if they do not need separate model calls.

Restricting the analysis to recent reviews roughly halved the workload. 197,827 eligible reviews, 100,611 from 2023–2026, and an estimated 95,640 after normalized-text deduplication. The final count is not a measured intersection.

If normalization is used to find duplicates, any returned phrase must also be checked against each original review.
These workload reductions are separate from the per-review savings. Filter only when the filter matches the analytical question, and reuse labels where doing so preserves the original records and their counts.

title: What LLM Summaries Miss in Customer Feedback
What LLM Summaries Miss in Customer Feedback
section: Two ways to turn comments into an overview
text:
Two ways to turn comments into an overview
The main benchmark was the test_syn portion of GermEval 2017: 2,095 German social and web posts about Deutsche Bahn. Human annotators had assigned topic categories to the posts, giving us a reference against which to check the models. After excluding the broad catch-all category Allgemein, 18 categories remained.
We called a category rare if it appeared in ten or fewer documents. Seven met that definition, ranging from QR codes in one document to accessibility in nine. These small categories form the long tail: issues that occur infrequently but may still matter to the people affected.
We compared two approaches. Corpus summarization asks the model to turn the collection into prose, either in one request or by summarizing chunks and then combining those summaries. Record-level labeling applies a known set of categories to each document separately and then aggregates the results.
The distinction is easiest to see with luggage, which appeared in two human-annotated documents. A summary might discuss luggage explicitly, fold it into a broad statement about comfort, or leave it out. A labeling system can attach the luggage category to the individual posts, allowing a reader to count and inspect them later. It can also get those labels wrong, so both approaches need checking.
For summaries, an LLM judge compared the final text with the human category inventory and classified each topic as clearly covered, vaguely covered, or absent. Positive verdicts required a supporting quotation. An independent audit checked those quotations and reproduced the aggregate results from the saved outputs, although some category matches remained open to interpretation.
For labeling, a rare category counted as preserved only if the model assigned it to at least one document that also carried that category in the human annotations. Emitting a label on an unrelated document did not count. This measures whether a topic survives somewhere in the output; it does not measure whether every relevant document was found or every assigned label was correct.

title: What LLM Summaries Miss in Customer Feedback
section: How many rare topics survived?
text:
How many rare topics survived?
The 15 GermEval summary variants clearly covered between one and three of the seven rare categories. The two labeling runs retained five and seven respectively: five with GPT-5.4 mini and seven with DeepSeek v4 flash.

Summaries preserved 1–3 rare topics; individual labels preserved 5–7. Observed ranges across 15 summary variants and two labeling runs. A topic survives in the labeling result only if at least one assigned document matches the human annotation.

A second benchmark showed the same direction. M-ABSA contained 538 short restaurant-review sentences and three rare categories. Its summaries clearly preserved between zero and two of those categories; all three labeling models retained at least one correct example of all three.
The main result is therefore about topic coverage, not overall model accuracy. Finding one correct luggage example keeps that category visible. It says nothing by itself about how many other luggage references the model missed or how often it applied the label incorrectly.

Travelling with children and toilets each appeared in seven documents, yet their outcomes differed sharply. Toilets received clear treatment in 13 summaries; travelling with children did so in only one. Frequency alone therefore does not explain which topics survived. Some issues may be easier to name distinctly, while others may be absorbed into broader themes, but this experiment does not isolate those causes.
Catering and design never received clear treatment. Every rare category was absent from at least one summary. By contrast, every category represented by 24 or more documents appeared at least vaguely in all 15 summaries. The summaries could capture the major themes while still providing an incomplete view of the smaller ones.

The QR-code example
The most extreme case was the category represented by a single document. Fourteen summaries omitted QR codes entirely. The fifteenth received credit for clear coverage because it mentioned “QR/PDF tickets” within a broader discussion of digital services. The audit flagged that verdict as borderline: the phrase named the subject, but did not clearly develop it as a distinct issue.
We retain the original score in the table and headline results. A stricter judgment would count no clear QR-code coverage at all. This illustrates why the difference between a passing mention and meaningful coverage needs to be visible to the reader.
The DeepSeek labeling run correctly labeled the source document; the other labeling model missed it. Individual labeling did not eliminate errors, but it left a result that could be checked against that specific post. A prose summary can also be audited, as we did here, but that requires returning to the source material to find out what is missing.

title: What LLM Summaries Miss in Customer Feedback
section: Can a better prompt or more context fix it?
text:
Can a better prompt or more context fix it?
The experiment tested more than a short request for the main themes. Summary prompts ranged from a basic management overview to a detailed inventory and an explicit request to preserve rare, minority, and contradictory views. Output targets were roughly 300 or 1,200 words; some responses exceeded those targets.
For larger workflows, we tested summarizing chunks and then combining their summaries, often called map-reduce. The variations included chunks of 50, 100, and 200 documents, as well as shuffled document order. We also tested putting all 2,095 documents into a single context, so there was no intermediate summary in which information could disappear.
The chart below focuses on the long-output prompt comparisons. Within this subset, no result clearly preserved more than two of the seven rare categories. The three-category maximum reported earlier came from another configuration in the broader experiment.

Explicit requests for rare issues did not consistently improve coverage. Long-output prompt comparisons. “Rare-aware” asks for rare, minority, and contradictory views. GPT-5.1 received the full corpus in one request; its detailed-inventory variant was not tested here.

With one run per configuration, these small differences are not a reliable ranking of prompt strategies. They do show that asking for rare issues was insufficient to produce a complete inventory in these tests.
The full-context result matters because it rules out one explanation for those particular omissions: nothing had been discarded by an earlier chunk summary. In a map-reduce workflow, that is an additional risk: a final summary that only sees intermediate summaries cannot reliably recover an issue they omitted. When all documents are available, omissions can still occur. These results establish that behavior; they do not establish the model’s internal reason for selecting some topics over others.

title: What LLM Summaries Miss in Customer Feedback
section: What the comparison can and cannot tell us
text:
What the comparison can and cannot tell us
The findings support a practical concern about completeness, with several limits on how far to take the numbers.
First, this was a comparison on two public benchmarks with known categories. It does not test whether a topic-discovery process would find every rare issue, or establish expected coverage for another industry or dataset. Labeling can only preserve a category if the schema provides somewhere for it to go.
Second, each summarization configuration was run once. The observed gap is worth investigating, but these ranges are not confidence intervals. More repeated runs would be needed to estimate how stable each configuration’s score is.
Third, the outputs and their scoring differ. A summary gets credit for clearly discussing a category; labeling gets credit for at least one correct document assignment. This provides a useful comparison of whether topics remain visible, but 100% category survival is not 100% labeling accuracy. Rare labels can still have low precision, meaning many documents assigned to a category do not belong there.
Finally, an LLM judged the summaries. Supporting quotations and an independent audit make those judgments inspectable, but they do not remove ambiguity. The QR-code example shows that even a quoted phrase can support more than one reasonable interpretation.

title: What LLM Summaries Miss in Customer Feedback
section: Keep the evidence before writing the overview
text:
Keep the evidence before writing the overview
A summary is useful when the task is to get oriented quickly. When the task involves counting issues, investigating small groups, or tracing a finding back to the people who raised it, the underlying records need to remain part of the analysis.
A practical workflow is to define or discover the categories, label each document, retain the source references, and check the resulting assignments. Counts and filters can then identify both common themes and smaller groups for closer inspection. The written overview comes after that evidence is available.


01 Define the categories Give distinct issues a place in the schema. Apply to each document


02 Label and retain evidence Keep each assignment linked to its source. Check assignments


03 Count and inspect Examine smaller groups as well as major themes. Select findings


04 Write the overview Explain the findings with counts and examples.


For the rail-feedback example, this means a reader can open the posts labeled as travelling with children and check what they say. If that topic is missing from the final overview, its evidence is still available. Checking a sample of the original posts also helps reveal issues the labeling step missed.
The goal is an overview whose omissions can be investigated. Keeping document-level evidence makes that possible without asking a few paragraphs to carry the entire dataset.

text:
Protect the strengths; distinguish the problems
Clinical bedside manner appears in 41.7% of labeled accounts, waiting in 26.2%, and front-desk conduct in 25.3%. These are the most frequently discussed topics, but their frequency does not tell us which response each needs.
The chart separates two questions: how often a topic appears, and how negatively it is described when it does. Together, they distinguish a widely valued aspect of the experience from recurring friction and smaller, consistently negative issues.

The most common topics are not the most consistently negative Each dot is one of the 29 topics. Select a topic for its exact values, or hover a dot. The dashed line marks the overall negative share among directional statements, 45.6%.

  ...chartBase(narrow ? 370 : 430),marginLeft:55,marginRight:22,marginBottom:55,
  x:{domain:[0,45],label:"Labeled reviews mentioning the topic (%)",grid:true,ticks:narrow ? 4 : 5},
  y:{domain:[0,100],label:"Negative statements (%)",grid:true,ticks:5},
  marks:[Plot.ruleY([45.5711599608296],{stroke:C.sub,strokeDasharray:"4,3"}),Plot.dot(topics,{x:"reach",y:"neg_share",r:5,fill:C.neutral,stroke:C.sub,tip:true,title:d=>`${d.topic}\nReach: ${d.reach.toFixed(2)}% of labeled reviews\nNegative: ${d.neg_share.toFixed(1)}% of directional statements`}),Plot.dot([focusedTopic],{x:"reach",y:"neg_share",r:8,fill:C.accent,stroke:C.ink,strokeWidth:1.5})]
})






Source: saved topic reach and sentiment aggregates. A review can mention several topics, so reach percentages do not add to 100%. Neutral statements are excluded from negative-share calculations.

Preserve clinical strengths. Only 20.9% of directional bedside-manner statements are negative. For a service lead, this is a reason to collect and share checked examples of listening, respect, and compassion in team learning and onboarding. It also leaves substantial negative feedback to understand: a common strength can still contain important exceptions.
Give recurring friction an operational owner. Waiting is the largest source of negative statements in the 29-topic framework, with 29,692. Together, waiting and front desk account for 25.8% of all negative statements. Front-desk tone is mostly positive, yet its large reach produces considerable negative volume. Put access and registration alongside clinical interactions on the patient-experience agenda, then identify the particular local process that needs to change.
Keep persistent and serious concerns visible. Billing appears in 4.6% of labeled accounts, but 93.6% of its directional statements are negative. Patient safety, privacy, and equitable-treatment topics also combine lower reach with strongly negative tone. A smaller volume is a reason for focused follow-up, rather than a reason to let an issue disappear behind the larger topics. Reports of harm or unfair treatment need human assessment through the hospital’s existing processes.
The practical priority is therefore not a single ranked list. Ask how much negative feedback an issue generates, how concentrated that negativity is, and whether the account describes something serious. Keep the strengths in view while deciding what to improve. These are complementary questions, not a formula for predicting the benefit of an intervention.


Explore every topic and the underlying taxonomy

section: A star average compresses experiences that need different responses
text:
A star average compresses experiences that need different responses
The sample’s 3.54-star average combines a polarized distribution: 89.2% of accounts give either one or five stars. An average is useful for tracking a summary, but this distribution tells a hospital team that the public record is dominated by strongly favorable and strongly unfavorable assessments.

One-star and five-star ratings account for 89.2% of reviews Share of the 217,343 sampled reviews at each rating. These are reviews, not extracted statements.

An overall assessment also does not describe every part of an account. In the labeled subset, 14,639 accounts (7.5%) contain both a positive and a negative topic statement. Among 64,283 labeled one-star accounts, 3,951 (6.1%) contain a positive topic statement.
Mixed feedback is a minority, but a measurable one. A low rating can identify a problem to resolve and a behavior to preserve. When learning from an account, separate those two contributions instead of treating every sentence as a complaint.
For reporting, show the rating distribution alongside the mean. For service recovery, identify the issue requiring a response while retaining any specific praise. For tracking change, use the same definitions and time window: a rising mean alone does not identify which process changed.

title: Patient Experience Through Hospital Reviews
section: Turn the findings into a small number of owned improvements
text:
Turn the findings into a small number of owned improvements
The findings support a practical agenda: preserve valued staff behaviors, give recurring access problems an operational response, and manage persistent financial concerns separately. Serious reported concerns should continue through their own human assessment route.
The table below translates that agenda into proposed next steps. The measures are examples to use locally; this study did not evaluate these interventions or their results.








Workstream and possible owner
Next step and evidence of progress




Access and registrationOperations/access and registration leads, with patient experience
Select one recurring wait or registration problem. Distinguish throughput, administrative completion, and interaction quality before choosing a change. Track: the relevant wait-stage or contact-completion measure, alongside topic-specific feedback over the same period.


Financial experiencePatient financial services and coverage/authorization team
Clarify ownership and the resolution route for charge disputes and coverage questions. Choose a locally supported process change. Track: resolution time, repeat contacts, recurring issue types, and financial-topic feedback.


Safety, privacy, and equitable treatmentThe hospital’s existing responsible teams
Retain a separate human assessment and escalation route, including lower-volume concerns. Track: validated case follow-up; assess seriousness from the account and appropriate evidence, independently of its star rating or topic volume.


Strengths in staff interactionsRelevant service/nursing leads and patient experience
Use checked examples of valued behaviors in team learning and onboarding, and preserve them during process changes. Track: feedback about those behaviors alongside appropriate local staff and patient evidence.




For the next improvement discussion, bring one recurring access issue and one persistent financial issue, each with an owner, a proposed change, and a measure that would show whether it helped. Choose the particular issues from the hospital’s own cases and service context. Keep the positive behaviors visible and serious concerns on their existing escalation route.
The reviewer-composition analysis examines whether contributor mix materially changes ratings. The topic-pair analysis identifies issues worth reading together, and the rating-association analysis asks which mentions remain associated with ratings after adjustment. Here, the useful outcome is an agenda with distinct questions and owners, rather than a single experience score expected to carry every decision.


Supporting detail: what the source material contains

The median sampled account contains 37 words, with a long tail of more detailed accounts. The length chart is retained here as context for the material being interpreted. Length itself does not establish seriousness or sentiment.

Most reviews are short, with a long tail
The median sampled review has 37 words. This density plot preserves the original distribution and its 2,500 sampled observation dots. The longest 1% of reviews, those exceeding 394 words, are omitted from this view. The vertical positions of the dots are jittered for visibility and do not encode sentiment or ratings.

Definitions, sources, and all original visualizations

Units. A review has one star rating and can contribute several labeled statements. Topic reach is the percentage of the 196,183 labeled reviews mentioning a topic at least once. Negative share is negative ÷ (negative + positive) statements. Negative statement volume counts label rows, rather than patients or care events. A statement has one topic in this accounting, so topic counts partition the 192,195 negative statements; reviews can mention several topics. Neutral statements are included in the 425,667 total but excluded from tone calculations.
Scope and sampling. The coverage sample was drawn from about 2.09 million eligible text reviews and contains 217,343 reviews of 10,029 U.S. healthcare listings, spanning 2019 to early June 2026. Sampling within listing and year, capped at 200 per listing, limits the influence of heavily reviewed locations. The 20-review minimum is source-listing eligibility, not a guarantee of 20 sampled or labeled accounts in every comparison. Unweighted results describe the sample. They do not represent all patients, care delivered, or total Google reviewing volume. Valid labels cover a narrower 9,904 listings. Collection ends in early June; 2026 is incomplete.
Label quality. Automated checks verify permitted topic names and IDs, quoted phrases, review resolution, and known sentiment. The saved report’s 98.8% mechanical validity rate is not human labeling accuracy. About 9.7% of sampled accounts have no retained statement; this summary does not establish why each was unlabelled. The 300-statement human audit is unfinished, so topic-level findings remain provisional. Serious labels describe reported concerns, rather than verified incidents.
New narrative calculations. Negative statement counts, within-topic 2022/2025 rates, and mixed-feedback counts were recomputed from the frozen label parquet using the same validity gates and distinct listing-plus-review keys. All 29 topic reach/tone values match the original chart snapshot. Mixed accounts have at least one valid positive and one negative statement; the one-star-with-praise figure requires at least one positive statement in a labeled one-star account. The annual contribution changes also match the saved chart data. Download the narrative evidence.
Trends and comparisons. A contribution divides a topic’s negative statement count by all directional statements that year. Its change combines topic mix and within-topic tone, with no adjustment for changing listings, services, or contributors. Listing cohorts are defined by first observed review year, not hospital opening date, and do not hold individual listings constant. State and category comparisons are unadjusted; platform categories can misdescribe services. Neither coefficients nor expected intervention benefits are estimated here.
Preserved figures and reproduction. Every original chart view, both maps, the full topic table, and their controls remain available on this page. The original exploratory report retains the additional taxonomy, treemap, city comparisons, topic bars, and rating gaps. Its stronger causal and care-quality interpretations are superseded by the wording here. Download the chart aggregates, map data, or new narrative evidence. The existing generator extracts saved chart outputs; the new evidence generator recomputes aggregates from frozen labels. Neither reruns a model or exports review text or contributor identifiers.

section: Financial concerns often need both charge and coverage context
text:
Financial concerns often need both charge and coverage context
Billing and insurance occur together in 908 low-rated reviews, about 4.6 times the shuffled comparison’s expected count of 199. More useful for follow-up is the asymmetry: 46% of insurance-related accounts also mention billing, while 12% of billing-related accounts mention insurance.







Starting set of low-rated feedback
Share also mentioning the other topic




Insurance: 1,989 reviews
908 also mention billing: 46%


Billing: 7,607 reviews
908 also mention insurance: 12%



The same 908 accounts sit behind both percentages. They answer different questions about context, not which problem came first. Coverage concerns often come with a description of charges; most charge-related feedback does not mention coverage. A hospital should therefore avoid treating every billing dispute as an insurance problem, while checking for financial context when examining coverage feedback.
This pairing largely reflects concerns about both subjects: 843 of the 908 accounts, or 93%, contain a negative statement about each. That check matters because a low overall rating does not make every topic mentioned a complaint.
The two categories also cover different issues. Billing includes unexpected or disputed charges, payment and collections; insurance includes coverage verification, denials, network and authorization. Reading the joint accounts can distinguish what was charged, what coverage decision was described, and what explanation was given. Those distinctions determine whether financial-services records, coverage or authorization records, or both are relevant.
For a hospital team, the practical lesson is to keep the charge and coverage descriptions together during follow-up. An accurate charge could still be poorly explained; a described coverage dispute needs different evidence from an alleged duplicate bill. These are questions to test against the full account and available records. The aggregate pairing does not identify which explanation applies or demonstrate a handoff failure.

title: How Problems Connect in Patient Feedback
section: Waiting feedback calls for different operational questions
text:
Waiting feedback calls for different operational questions
Waiting and staffing/operational capacity appear together in 2,075 low-rated reviews, about 1.36 times the shuffled expectation. Waiting is mentioned in 47% of capacity-related feedback, but capacity appears in only 9% of waiting feedback. These shares use 4,398 capacity-related and 22,622 waiting-related reviews as their respective denominators.
The distinction changes the question a hospital should ask. Capacity concerns often come with delays, but most waiting feedback does not explicitly describe a capacity constraint. The “staffing” label in the charts covers beds, equipment and overcrowding as well as personnel. It measures what people describe, rather than actual staffing levels, and cannot justify a general recommendation to hire more staff.
In 2,042 of the 2,075 paired accounts, or 98%, both topics have a negative statement. This gives an operations team a focused set of jointly described concerns to examine. The useful next step is to locate the waiting stage and the reported constraint: arrival, testing, admission or another part of care. Available demand, resource and stage-specific waiting records can then help assess whether that description fits an operational bottleneck. Explanations given during the wait belong in the same reading, since a reported constraint and uncertainty about a delay require different follow-up.
Administrative experiences offer a useful contrast. Front-desk conduct and waiting appear together in 4,436 low-rated reviews, more than twice the capacity/waiting count. Yet this pairing is not unusually concentrated under the comparison model: its independently calculated lift is about 0.96. A large recurring set of concerns can deserve attention even when it is absent from the retained association map.
That is why volume, concentration and seriousness need separate judgments. Counts help locate a substantial body of feedback. Lift helps identify relationships that appear more often than the comparison predicts. The full account and corroborating evidence determine the significance of a particular concern. Neither a large count nor a high lift estimates the benefit of an intervention.

title: How Problems Connect in Patient Feedback
section: Smaller connected concerns deserve specific follow-up
text:
Smaller connected concerns deserve specific follow-up
Behavioral health and discrimination/equitable treatment appear together in 212 low-rated reviews, roughly twice the shuffled expectation. 203 of these accounts, or 96%, contain a negative statement about both topics. The lower volume does not settle how significant the described experiences may be.
The value of the pairing is a narrower reading question: how are the treatment setting and the interaction perceived as unfair described together? Among these 212 accounts, 51 also mention bedside manner, 34 medication and 32 safety. These overlapping subsets suggest additional context to check in particular accounts; they do not show that everyone describes the same set of problems.
A service or patient-experience team could use this selection to examine the reported interaction, what treatment or explanation was described, and what would need verification. Relevant concerns can then enter the appropriate existing service, experience or quality process. The model’s categories do not establish a diagnosis, the author’s role, verified discrimination or a safety incident.
The learning is to preserve the specific concern when summarizing smaller categories. A broad “staff experience” summary could obscure the question of perceived fairness. A network group cannot determine seriousness or ownership on its own; those decisions need human reading and appropriate supporting evidence.

section: Turn a connection into a better investigation
text:
Turn a connection into a better investigation
The practical output is a more specific question and the context needed to answer it. Start by validating the labels and reading each selected account in full. Identify the uncertainty before choosing participants or requesting records. The examples suggest different follow-up needs:








Linked concerns
Context to preserve
Question and evidence for follow-up




Billing with insurance
Charges, coverage decisions and the explanation described
What was disputed or unclear? Which financial and coverage records, and which teams, can assess it?


Waiting with capacity
Waiting stage, reported resource constraint and communication
Do available process, demand and capacity records support the described bottleneck, or point to a different question?


Behavioral health with equitable treatment
Treatment setting, interaction and perceived unfairness
What needs human verification, and which existing service, experience or quality process should receive it?



Keep the linked context attached if the concern moves between teams. If an investigation leads to a process change, assess that change using independent process and experience evidence. A shift in the number of public co-mentions alone cannot establish improvement: participation, listing mix and the language people use may also change.
The connections help choose what to examine together. They do not establish escalation over time or an extra combined rating penalty. The supporting checks below explain those limits and why topic-level sentiment must be checked even in highly rated feedback.


Why a connected pair does not establish an extra rating penalty

The separate rating-association model examines five selected pairs of negative topic mentions, accounting for other topic mentions, review length, year, reviewer group, total topic count and listing effects. In held-out listings, all five interaction estimates are positive: the combined rating association is less negative than adding the two separate associations would predict. This model therefore does not support a beyond-additive negative rating claim for these pairs.

The follow-up model did not find an additional negative rating interaction Five selected pairs in held-out listings. Dots are interaction estimates; intervals are 95% confidence intervals clustered by listing. A negative estimate would indicate an additional penalty beyond the model’s separate associations.

A positive interaction does not mean two problems are good or less serious. It concerns an additive rating model on a scale bounded below by one star; that bound may contribute to the pattern, but its role is not established here. Neither this model nor the pair map evaluates the effect of fixing a problem.



Why high ratings do not automatically mean positive experiences

The saved comparison finds 16 qualifying pairs in four- and five-star feedback, versus 31 in one- and two-star feedback; 11 appear in both sets. It uses 299 shuffles for the high-rating analysis and 499 for the low-rating analysis.

Billing and insurance also appear together in 58 high-rated accounts. Of those, 21 contain a negative statement about both topics and 21 contain a positive statement about both; sentiment flags can overlap. A high overall rating does not establish satisfaction with every aspect of the experience. Check the text and topic-level sentiment before selecting examples of successful handling for learning.
The 20 pairs qualifying only in low-rated feedback are candidates for closer reading, rather than complaint-exclusive patterns. Behavioral health and equitable treatment, for example, also occur together in 26 high-rated accounts, below the 30-co-mention testing threshold. Absence from the qualifying list cannot establish absence from the feedback. These comparisons do not formally test whether associations differ between rating bands.



Supporting plots, methods and aggregate data

Scope and labels. The year- and listing-stratified coverage sample contains 217,343 reviews from 2019 to early June 2026. Of these, 196,183 have at least one label passing automated topic, quoted-phrase, review-ID and sentiment checks. Within the 72,038 labeled one- and two-star reviews, 47,405 mention at least two distinct topics. Reviews are keyed by listing plus review ID and counted once per topic. Healthcare listings are not necessarily distinct hospitals. Automated validity checks do not replace the pending human label audit, and topic labels describe reported experiences rather than verified events.
Comparison. Topic columns are independently shuffled 499 times within original topic-count strata (2, 3, 4, 5+), skipping strata below 50 reviews. This preserves each topic’s stratum-level frequency, but not exact word length or every shuffled row’s topic count. Pairs with at least 30 observed co-mentions are tested; retention requires a Benjamini–Hochberg q-value below 0.05 and lift above 1.15. Greedy modularity groups the network using log₂ lift as the weight. Group names are editorial; stability across alternative clustering algorithms is not established.
New descriptive checks. Conditional shares divide co-mentions by all labeled reviews in the rating band mentioning the starting topic. A topic has a negative or positive flag when any validity-gated statement has that sentiment; flags can overlap. Co-mentions in the original screen can have any sentiment. The focal sentiment checks support interpreting these particular low-rated pairs as joint concerns, rather than establishing that every pair is jointly negative. Exact shuffle expectations reconcile the saved retained-pair lifts to within 1.28%; the charts retain their original finite-shuffle estimates. No statistical screen or interaction model is refitted.
Preserved analyses. The earlier exploratory report retains the unadjusted severity comparison, facility-category checks and monthly and pandemic-period series. Read its unadjusted ratings alongside the adjusted model above; causal or compound-penalty interpretations are not supported by these findings. The executed notebook reports mean correlations of monthly attention changes of 0.119 within groups versus −0.001 across groups; corresponding tone correlations are 0.105 versus 0.091. These exploratory summaries do not independently validate the grouping or establish an early-warning system. Listing mix and the single pandemic period complicate interpretation.
Downloads and reproducibility. Download the original aggregate chart data and the additional counts, conditional shares and sentiment checks. The chart generator extracts saved report aggregates and imports the later model’s holdout estimates. The additional evidence is recomputed from the frozen coverage and label parquet files by scripts/generate_hospital_pair_insights.py. These exports contain no raw review text or reviewer identifiers.

For the companion sensitivity analysis, see Whose Voices Shape Hospital Ratings.

title: Make the Next Step Clear
text:
Patients can leave an appointment with information and still feel uncertain about what happens next. At one U.S. hospital in our sample, communication stands out in the positive feedback: people describe explanations they could understand, questions they could ask, and a clearer sense of the plan. Those accounts suggest practical habits a hospital team can build into everyday care.
The hospital, anonymised here as Hospital A, has communication praise in 26 of 104 labeled reviews from 2023–2025. That is 25.0%, compared with 8.2% across other listings in the same Google category. The difference remains when we compare only positive ratings and when we restrict those positive accounts to longer texts.
The useful lesson lies in what the praise describes. A patient explains that staff made the course of treatment understandable. Another describes questions being answered while their comfort received attention. A third describes leaving a discussion about the care plan feeling more relieved than on arrival. These are de-identified paraphrases of separate accounts.
They point to a practical purpose for communication: help a person understand the situation, participate in it, and know what comes next. A hospital can use that purpose to choose a specific improvement and assess whether patients notice a difference.
This exploratory case uses sampled public feedback. Its benchmark contains 26,561 labeled reviews at other listings categorised as hospitals, with differences in services and patient populations still unresolved. The wider automated labels remain provisional pending human validation. The case identifies reported strengths and practices to test.

title: Make the Next Step Clear
section: Find a strength specific enough to learn from
text:
Find a strength specific enough to learn from
Hospital A’s higher average rating would be an incomplete reason to study its communication. A hospital receiving more positive feedback has more opportunities to receive praise of every kind. The more useful question is whether communication remains distinctive among accounts that are already favorable.
It does. Among 4–5-star reviews, 26.8% at Hospital A praise communication, compared with 12.5% at other hospital-category listings. Among those positive reviews containing at least 25 words, the shares are 43.2% and 16.7%. The longer-text comparison matters because a brief endorsement offers less room to describe an explanation or a conversation.

The gap also appears in each of the three years. It gives us a consistent reason to examine the accounts closely, though it cannot explain why the difference exists. Specialty care, expectations, and who chooses to contribute may still matter.
For a hospital learning from a positive example, this is a useful starting rule: choose a particular strength, then identify the behaviours behind it. A broad instruction to emulate a highly rated hospital leaves a team with little to change. Explanations, opportunities for questions, and understandable plans are more specific subjects for improvement.

title: Make the Next Step Clear
section: Explain the step the patient is about to take
text:
Explain the step the patient is about to take
In a manual reading of all 26 communication-positive accounts, 13 describe explanations of steps, procedures, results or the care plan. The situations differ, but the recurring value is being able to follow what is happening.
One account describes explanations across the course of care. Another describes understanding what was happening and what would happen next. A further account describes a discussion that produced a plan for the months ahead. These examples locate communication at particular moments when a patient needs to make sense of the experience.
The practical learning is to build explanations into transitions. Moving to a test, waiting for results, or leaving with follow-up arrangements each creates a new question for the patient. A team could choose one transition and make three things explicit: the immediate next step, what the patient needs to do, and where to take an unanswered question.
That is a proposed application of the accounts, rather than a verified Hospital A protocol. Its value can be tested directly: after the transition, can the patient explain what happens next? If people remain uncertain, the team has a specific communication gap to address, even when the appointment ran on time.

title: Make the Next Step Clear
section: Make understanding part of the conversation
text:
Make understanding part of the conversation
Four accounts explicitly praise explanations in language the person could understand. Their point is more specific than receiving information: the explanation made sense to the recipient.
Fifteen accounts describe answers to questions or listening to concerns and preferences. These groups overlap with the explanations above. Together, they suggest a conversation in which patients can contribute what they need clarified, as well as hear what staff need to tell them.
For a service lead, the practical question is whether the patient leaves with an understandable plan and space to resolve uncertainty. A team could invite the person’s remaining questions and ask them to describe the next step in their own words. That would make a misunderstanding visible while there is still an opportunity to clarify it.
The appropriate local measure is therefore patient understanding. Counting completed explanations would document an activity; checking whether people can describe the plan would test whether it served its purpose. Both may be useful, but they answer different questions.

title: Make the Next Step Clear
section: Look for the experience an explanation supports
text:
Look for the experience an explanation supports
Six of the 26 accounts describe comfort, ease, relief, feeling heard, or not feeling rushed. One combines answered questions with attention to physical and emotional comfort. Another describes relief after discussing the plan. These accounts connect information with how the person experienced the encounter.
That connection gives communication a possible role across several areas of patient experience. An explanation of a delay could help someone understand the wait. A clear discussion at discharge could help them understand follow-up. Time to raise concerns could help someone feel heard.
These are hypotheses a hospital could test. The case does not show that explanations shortened waits, reduced anxiety on a measured scale, or prevented follow-up problems. The topic comparisons also provide no evidence of a general improvement in bedside-manner praise alongside communication praise.
The useful distinction is between a shared account and a demonstrated improvement. We can observe that some people describe explanations alongside relief or comfort. To learn whether changing a communication practice improves those experiences, a hospital needs a defined change and measures before and after it, with a suitable comparison where possible.
For waiting, that means tracking both the time elapsed and whether people understood the delay and the next update. For discharge, it means checking both completion of the process and understanding of the follow-up plan. An improvement in either experience should be described in terms of what was actually measured.

title: Make the Next Step Clear
section: Start with one transition and a clear test
text:
Start with one transition and a clear test
The case gives a hospital team a manageable place to begin: one service, one transition, and one patient need that is currently unclear. The goal is to make that part of care easier to understand.








Place to start
Practice to test
Evidence that would show whether it helped




Before a test or procedure
Explain the immediate next step and invite questions
Whether patients understand what happens next and report unresolved questions


During a delay
Explain what is known and agree when the next update will come
Whether patients felt informed, alongside the actual waiting time


At discharge or follow-up planning
Discuss the plan in plain language and check understanding
Whether patients can describe their next action and know where to seek clarification



These applications extend the needs described in the case; the study has not evaluated them. A bounded pilot should record when the practice changed and compare similar services and periods. Patient feedback can then sit alongside operational records and a short, consistent check of understanding. Changes in review volume or service mix also need attention before an improved public rating is treated as evidence of success.
Hospital A’s contribution is a concrete example of what people value in communication: explanations that make sense, questions that receive attention, and a plan they can follow. Another hospital can use those needs to choose a practice, give it an owner, and test whether patients leave the selected transition better informed.


Data, case selection and supporting checks

Source and units. The wider study contains 217,343 sampled Google reviews from 2019 to early June 2026. Of these, 196,183 have at least one topic label passing four mechanical validity checks and a recognised sentiment value. This article uses complete calendar years 2023–2025. A communication-positive flag records at least one valid positive label for “Communication and information sharing.” Each listing-plus-review key counts once; repeated statements do not increase its weight in the displayed percentages.
Case and benchmark. Hospital A was selected after exploring 22 listings categorised as Hospital, General hospital or University hospital with at least 100 labeled reviews in the selected period, followed by closer reading of several candidates. It had the highest communication-praise share in that eligible set. Selection used the same data as the comparison, so this is an exploratory example, not a validated performance ranking. The benchmark excludes Hospital A and contains 26,561 labeled reviews across 2,075 listings with the exact Google category “Hospital,” matching its platform category. Listings can combine inpatient, outpatient and specialty encounters; category matching does not equalise service mix or patient characteristics.
Sensitivity checks. Communication praise appears in 6/36, 13/42 and 7/26 case reviews in 2023, 2024 and 2025, respectively. The corresponding benchmark shares are 524/7,452, 639/7,977 and 1,016/11,132. Sampling weights yield rates of 25.0% at Hospital A and 8.6% in the benchmark. Giving peer rates Hospital A’s exact rating and three review-length-bin composition yields an expected 9.9%, compared with 25.0% observed. These checks address particular aspects of the comparison; they do not remove review self-selection or establish a causal difference. Service-specific case counts are too small to resolve service mix.
Reading the accounts. All 26 communication-positive case accounts were read and conservatively coded for recurring behaviours and experiences. Categories overlap. Thirteen describe explanations of steps, procedures, results or the plan; 15 describe answers or listening; four explicitly praise understandable language; six mention comfort, ease, relief, being heard or not feeling rushed; two explicitly include family in updates or answers. This reading covers a model-selected case subset, not an independent audit of the full labeling dataset. The same behaviours have not yet been coded in a matched peer sample, so their comparative prevalence is unknown.
Other-topic overlap. Bedside-manner praise appears in 11 of the 26 communication-positive accounts and 41 of the other 78 accounts. Its rate is therefore not higher in the communication-positive group. This descriptive overlap does not establish a beneficial or harmful communication effect; differences in what people emphasise and how statements are classified may matter.
Interpretation and anonymity. Labels describe the text accompanying a rating. Mechanical checks establish source matching, not human agreement with every classification. Public contributors are self-selected and are not a representative patient survey. No intervention date, staff protocol, measured anxiety, waiting records or clinical outcomes were established for Hospital A. Recommendations are proposed local applications. Patient examples are paraphrased with identifying details removed; none is a quotation or a composite presented as an observed account.
Download the anonymous aggregate evidence. The broader hospital analysis examines strengths and recurring friction across the full sample; the topic-pair analysis examines which subjects appear together.
